posts.title: Sequence changes and permanent connections: CROSS 1588 learning for contractors
posts.excerpt: CROSS-UK Report 1588 (3 November 2026) records a proposed change on a 60 m steel girder bridge from sequential in-situ splicing of paired lifts to a single ground-spliced lift. The change altered loads through bolted splice connections intended to remain friction-grip. Review by the permanent works designer before the lift identified the conflict. Contractors must route sequence changes through the Temporary Works Coordinator and confirm permanent works assumptions under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015.
posts.linkedinReady:
A change to the lift sequence can change the permanent connection behaviour the designer assumed.

CROSS-UK Report 1588 (published 3 November 2026) describes a proposed change on a 60 m steel girder bridge. The permanent works designer had designed for three girder sections to be braced in pairs, lifted, and spliced sequentially in situ. The contractor, with their temporary works designer, proposed splicing the sections on the ground and making a single lift, with lifting points near the splices. That change altered the loads expected through the bolted splice connections.

The permanent works review found that the single-lift method relied on the connection plates shifting to engage the bolts in end bearing. The connections were intended to maintain a friction-grip (slip-resistant) behaviour. Movement at the faying surfaces during the lift could have damaged those surfaces, reducing long-term slip resistance and potentially affecting fatigue performance over the 120-year design life. The bridge may have remained stable during erection; the permanent performance could still have been compromised. The issue was identified because the contractor’s engineering team followed the review processes in BS 5975 and PAS 8811 and engaged the permanent works designer before construction started.

For contractors the control is the interface. Anyone specifying or modifying a construction method assumes designer duties under CDM 2015. Sequence changes that affect load path, restraint or connection behaviour must be referred back to the permanent works designer before they are implemented. The Temporary Works Coordinator coordinates that interface, keeps the item on the Temporary Works Register, and confirms that the temporary works design brief captures the permanent works assumptions that matter.

body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1588 (published 3 November 2026) records a proposed change to the construction sequence for erection of a 60 m steel girder bridge. The Permanent Works Designer (PWD) had designed the bridge on the basis that three girder sections would be braced in pairs, lifted, and spliced sequentially in situ after installation onto the bridge supports. The Contractor, working with their Temporary Works Designer (TWD), proposed instead to splice the three sections together on the ground and undertake a single lift. The lifting points for the single fully spliced girder were located near the spliced connections. The proposed change altered the loads expected to be transferred through the splice connections during installation. A review of the single lift by the PWD highlighted changes to key design assumptions in the superstructure calculation report concerning the expected performance of the bolted splice connection. The single lifting operation relied on the connection plates at the splice locations shifting during the lift to engage the bolts in end bearing. The PWD review determined that these connections were intended to maintain a friction-grip connection. Had the single lift proceeded without PWD challenge, movement at the splice interfaces could have damaged the prepared faying surfaces, reducing the long-term slip resistance of the splice connections. While the bridge may have remained stable during erection, the permanent structural performance could have been compromised, with potential impact on long-term fatigue performance over the structure’s 120-year design life. The issue was identified only because the Contractor’s engineering team followed the review processes recommended in BS 5975 and PAS 8811 and engaged with the Permanent Works Designer before construction commenced.

Temporary conditions during construction can be more onerous than the completed structure, and connections are frequently critical elements that also form the interface between different designers. A connection designed for a particular behaviour in the completed structure should not be assumed to behave the same way during erection. Changing the erection methodology changed the way forces would be transferred through the girder splice connections. Under CDM 2015, anyone who specifies or modifies a construction method assumes designer responsibilities and must consider the consequences for both temporary and permanent works. BS 5975-1:2024 provides the framework for managing the interface, including the responsibilities of the permanent works designer. Critical design assumptions (in this case the long-term slip-resistant behaviour of the splices) were documented in the calculations but were not explicitly communicated through a risk register or clear notes on a drawing. The temporary works management process provided the opportunity to identify the conflict before the lift. Contractors therefore need a controlled route for any proposed sequence change that could affect load path, restraint, connection behaviour or permanent works assumptions.

ul: Treat proposed changes to erection sequence, lift configuration or splicing order as temporary works items that require review against the permanent works design assumptions. Enter or update the item on the Temporary Works Register. Provisional category only — to be confirmed under the project procedure; escalate where connections, load path or long-term permanent performance are affected.

Require a design brief that records the permanent works assumptions that matter for the temporary condition (connection type and intended behaviour, permitted loads, sequence constraints, faying surface protection) and the proposed change.

Do not implement a sequence change that alters loading, restraint or connection behaviour until the permanent works designer has reviewed the implications and any necessary design measures have been accepted.

Confirm that the temporary works design package addresses both the temporary stability of the lift and the effect on the permanent connections. A practical lift that remains stable during erection can still damage surfaces or change the behaviour the permanent design relies on.
Coordinate the interface formally. The Temporary Works Coordinator ensures the permanent works designer is engaged and that the design responsibility matrix is clear before the change proceeds.
Hold points for review of the revised method and acceptance of the temporary works before any ground splicing or single lift is permitted.

body.p: The BBC published on 20 November 2026 that the Health and Safety Executive has said it is working urgently to help make the site of a partial building collapse safe. An apartment block under construction on the A4260 Cherwell Street in Banbury partly collapsed alongside scaffolding on 21 October. Thames Valley Police reported nine workers on site at the time, with two taken to hospital. A local councillor had accused HSE of holding the town to ransom over delays in the clear-up. An HSE spokesperson responded that it was “working urgently with the contractors on site as they seek to make it safe”, that the road closure is a matter for the local council, and that HSE realises this is a difficult situation for residents and businesses. Cherwell District Council’s inspectors had found the building presented a significant risk of further structural failure. Protective fencing was installed to mitigate the risk of falling debris. The lanes furthest from the site are open; those closer remain closed until the site is made safe. No published statement establishes the cause of the original collapse.

A partial collapse of a building under construction and its scaffolding leaves a residual risk of further failure. The works required to make the site safe — temporary support, exclusion, controlled dismantling or stabilisation — are temporary works. They must be managed under the project temporary works procedure and BS 5975-1:2024. CDM 2015 Regulation 19 requires that all practicable steps are taken to ensure that any new or existing structure does not collapse if, due to the carrying out of construction work, it may become unstable or is in a temporary state of weakness or instability. Any temporary support must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads and used only for the purpose for which it was designed. HSE’s investigation and its advice to the contractor sit alongside, not instead of, the principal contractor’s duties to plan, manage and monitor the work and to appoint a competent Temporary Works Coordinator where required. Public interface and exclusion zones remain part of that control until the permanent condition is restored and accepted.

ul: Treat all making-safe works (propping, bracing, exclusion fencing, controlled removal) as temporary works items on the Temporary Works Register. Provisional category only — to be confirmed under the project procedure; escalate where residual collapse risk, public interface or incomplete structure are present.

Require a design brief that records the current condition of the structure and scaffold, residual risks identified by inspection, loads the temporary supports must carry, exclusion zones, sequence of works and the criteria for acceptance before any reduction in exclusion.
Do not rely on an earlier design or inspection once the structure has changed. A post-collapse condition needs a fresh assessment of load path and stability.
Coordinate with the local authorities on public exclusion and road management, but do not treat a highway decision as a substitute for a competent temporary works acceptance.
Hold points for inspection after any temporary support is installed and before any further loading, dismantling or public access is restored.
Close the temporary works item only when the structure has been verified as stable without the temporary measures, or when the measures have been formally accepted as the residual control.

body.p: Ground Engineering published on 20 November 2026 an account of Manchester City Council’s works on Alan Turing Way. A depression in the road surface in late March 2026 led to closure of the northbound carriageway between Ashton Old Road and Grey Mare Lane. Initial speculation of a utility failure was superseded by specialist investigations that identified an unrecorded historical mine shaft. A Manchester City Council spokesperson told GE that the area was investigated through a shored excavation approximately 6.4 m by 6.3 m in extent, with soft made ground recorded to about 6 m below ground level. A smaller area of around 3 m by 2 m immediately beneath the initial feature contained a greater thickness of made ground. Ground investigation and treatment works were complicated by the depth of the excavation and by United Utilities and Openreach infrastructure across the hole. Ground investigation was completed in the surrounding area and from a drilling platform constructed over the excavation. Rotary percussive probe holes, including inclined probes, from that platform identified an approximately 3 m diameter mine shaft extending to 50 m below ground level, with mine workings at about 40 m. The Mining Remediation Authority completed desktop research on 1 June 2026 and determined the issue was not coal-mining related. Stabilisation work between 17 September and early October pumped more than 100 t of grout into the shaft and surrounding ground, added loose shaft backfill to the level of the top of the glacial till, and installed a 550 mm thick reinforced concrete cap over the shaft. Foam concrete and stone reinstated levels within the initial excavation. Road reconstruction is expected to allow reopening by early to mid-December.

The shored excavation and the drilling platform constructed over it are temporary works. They support plant, people and investigation loads above and beside an unrecorded deep void in soft made ground, with live utility apparatus crossing the works. Until the permanent cap and reinstatement are complete and accepted, residual risk of further ground movement or collapse remains. CDM 2015 Regulation 19 requires that a structure be stable and capable of withstanding the loads to which it is subjected during construction. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out the management procedures (register, design brief, design check, TWC/TWS roles, permits) that demonstrate those duties are being met for temporary works. A public-highway interface and buried services raise the consequence of failure. The fact that the Mining Remediation Authority concluded the feature was not coal-mining related does not remove the need for a temporary works design brief that covers the actual ground conditions, the platform loading, the shoring system and the sequence of grouting and capping.

ul: Enter the shored excavation and the drilling platform as separate or linked items on the Temporary Works Register. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure; escalate where deep voids, soft ground, live services or public interface are present.

Require a design brief that records excavation geometry, ground conditions (including soft made ground thickness), plant and surcharge loads on the platform, buried services clearances, exclusion zones and the residual risk until the permanent cap is in place and verified.
Verify the load path for the drilling platform: how loads are transferred into competent ground or supported across the excavation without relying on the void or unpropped soft ground.

Coordinate with utility owners (United Utilities, Openreach) for temporary support, protection or diversion of apparatus crossing the excavation. Do not treat service crossings as outside the temporary works scope.
Inspect shoring and the platform after any change in ground conditions, rainfall, or additional plant. Do not reuse an earlier inspection once the sequence has moved to grouting or capping.
Do not proceed with excavation, platform loading, grouting or capping until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: What the highway authority then decided
body.p: Oxfordshire County Council published a highways update at 13:16 UK time on 18 November 2026. It said Cherwell Street had to close overnight on 17/18 November after a Cherwell District Council safety inspection showed that the condition of the collapsed scaffolding had further deteriorated. The county council said work had been undertaken to address that issue and that the route can reopen to both northbound and southbound traffic. Northbound use is to resume from the afternoon of Thursday 19 November. Part of the normal road space will remain unavailable because of its immediate proximity to the scaffolding site. The same note records the earlier sequence: the road closed on 21 October when the scaffolding collapse occurred; it was partially opened both ways late on 30 October after Cherwell District Council advised that this could safely happen; and from the evening of Wednesday 11 November the open section was designated southbound only, with northbound traffic diverted via George Street, Marlborough Road, Horse Fair and North Bar Street, and Lower Cherwell Street restricted to a left turn onto Cherwell Street. The county statement does not withdraw the district council’s finding of significant risk of further structural failure. It is a decision about traffic, after work on the deteriorated scaffold, with a reduced carriageway left in place beside the site.

A scaffold that has already collapsed, and a building the local authority has assessed as presenting a significant risk of further structural failure, are not a completed permanent-works condition. Until the structure can stand without temporary support and the investigation is closed, stability, exclusion and the public interface remain temporary works matters under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015. The new public facts are the further deterioration, the precautionary closure, the fencing against falling debris, the advice to the neighbouring garage and flats, and a partial reopening that still keeps road space out of use beside the scaffold. None of those statements gives a cause for the 21 October collapse, and none should be read as a design check or a permit to load, alter or strike any remaining scaffold. Where a damaged temporary structure stands next to a live highway, the consequence of a further failure includes people who are not on the site. That is why the exclusion zone, the inspection by a competent person, and a current decision under the project temporary works procedure matter more than the traffic bulletin.

ul: Treat a collapsed or deteriorated scaffold, and any incomplete structure it is tied to or standing against, as still inside the temporary works procedure. Do not assume a highway reopening means the structure has been accepted as stable.
Keep a physical exclusion zone that matches the current risk of falling debris, including neighbouring premises and parked vehicles, and record who set it and on what inspection.
Re-inspect after any further deterioration, high wind, or making-safe works, and do not reuse an inspection from before the condition changed.

Separate the traffic management decision from the temporary works decision. A reduced carriageway beside the scaffold is a remaining public interface, not evidence that the scaffold can be altered, loaded or removed.

Do not publish or adopt a cause. The 21 October collapse remains without a published finding. Briefings and toolbox talks should stay with the controls: design brief, competent inspection, register, permit and interface with the permanent works.
Do not proceed with erection, alteration, loading or striking until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

posts.title: CIRIA Report 108 and modern concretes: formwork pressure assumptions require project-specific review
posts.excerpt: A 9 November 2026 discussion of the Temporary Works Forum’s June 2026 quarterly meeting highlights that low-carbon, self-consolidating and rheotropic concretes can hydrate more slowly and remain fluid longer than the mixes underlying CIRIA Report 108. Rate-of-rise charts may therefore understate formwork pressure. Site practices such as high-pressure pumping, bottom-up placing and re-energising lower lifts compound the risk. Temporary Works Coordinators must obtain mix-specific data, align pour rates with the design basis, and consider monitoring or independent checking before falsework is accepted under the project temporary works procedure.
posts.linkedinReady:
Formwork pressure calculations based on CIRIA Report 108 assume concrete behaviour that modern low-carbon mixes do not always follow.

CIRIA Report 108 (Clear and Harrison, 1985) remains the common UK method for estimating concrete pressure on formwork. It was calibrated to site measurements of the concretes then in use. At the Temporary Works Forum’s 66th quarterly meeting in June 2026, practitioners discussed the impact of modern ultra-low-carbon, low-heat, self-consolidating and rheotropic mixes. These can show slower hydration, altered temperature profiles and extended fluid behaviour, so the point at which the concrete stops acting as a fluid can shift. Rate-of-rise assumptions may therefore understate pressure even when the programme pour rate is unchanged.

Site practices already known to drive pressures higher—over-compaction or re-energising lower lifts, high-pressure pumping, bottom-up placing, irregular rates and delays between lifts—compound the issue when combined with slower-setting mixes. The Temporary Works Forum session left the question open: revised guidance has not yet been published.

For principal contractors and Temporary Works Coordinators the practical steps are clear before any falsework design is accepted:

- Obtain the actual mix design, binder blend, setting-time and heat-development data from the supplier rather than relying on a generic low-carbon label.
- Confirm that the pour rate, placing method and any re-energising practices used in the calculation match what will be used on site.
- Treat a mix whose behaviour sits outside the CIRIA 108 calibration population as a case for independent design check.
- Where monitoring is feasible, link the falsework design to a plan for real-time pressure or maturity data so deviations are visible before a problem develops.
- Enter the falsework on the Temporary Works Register with the correct category and ensure it is designed, checked and permitted under the project procedure and BS 5975-1:2024 / BS 5975-2:2024.

CDM 2015 Regulation 19 and HSE temporary-works guidance require temporary structures to be designed, installed and maintained for the loads they will actually see. Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: A practitioner note published on 9 November 2026 summarises discussion at the Temporary Works Forum’s 66th quarterly meeting (June 2026 at the Institution of Civil Engineers). Aaron Lucid of Vemaventuri GmbH (a PERI partner) presented on the impact of modern concretes on CIRIA Report 108 rate-of-rise assumptions. The session reviewed CIRIA 108 assumptions on rate of rise, temperature and concrete grouping against today’s mix designs. Modern ultra-low-carbon and low-heat concretes were described as showing slower hydration, altered temperature profiles and extended fluid behaviour that challenge traditional pressure envelopes. Self-consolidating and rheotropic mixes bring thixotropy, prolonged hydrostatic conditions and non-linear solidification rates. Site practices that can drive pressures beyond model expectations—over-compaction or re-energising lower lifts, high-pressure pumping and bottom-up placing, irregular pour rates and delays between lifts—were also highlighted. The stated aim was to prompt discussion on whether current use of CIRIA Report 108 remains conservative for modern and ultra-low-carbon concretes and how monitoring data should inform future guidance. No revised published guidance has closed the question.

CIRIA Report 108 (Clear & Harrison, 1985) is the established UK method for estimating concrete pressure on formwork. It was derived from a programme of site measurements and applies coefficients that reflect the concretes and placing practices of that period. Where a modern mix remains fluid longer than the calibration population assumed, design pressure at a given height can exceed the chart value even if the nominal rate of rise is unchanged. Falsework and formwork are temporary works that must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads (HSE temporary-works guidance; CDM 2015 Regulation 19). An understated pressure is a load-path and stability risk for the formwork system, ties, props and supporting falsework. The Temporary Works Coordinator is the person who must ensure suitable designs are prepared, checked and correctly erected. Treating the CIRIA method as automatically conservative for every low-carbon or self-consolidating mix without mix-specific verification is not supported by the open discussion at the TWf meeting.

ul: Obtain the actual mix design (binder blend, admixtures, target strength) and supplier data on setting time and heat development before the falsework design is finalised. Do not rely on a generic “low-carbon” label.

Confirm that the rate of rise, placing method (including any bottom-up or high-pressure pumping) and any planned re-energising or over-compaction practices used in the pressure calculation match the intended site method.

Where the mix behaviour is outside the population for which CIRIA Report 108 was calibrated, treat independent design checking as essential rather than discretionary and record the check on the Temporary Works Register.

Consider whether real-time monitoring (embedded pressure or maturity sensors) should form part of the design package so that actual pressures can be compared with the calculated envelope during the pour.

Enter the formwork/falsework on the live Temporary Works Register with the correct provisional design and check category, brief the designer against the confirmed mix and pour parameters, and issue a permit only after the arrangement has been accepted under the project temporary works procedure.
Do not allow the pour to proceed if the design basis (mix data, rate of rise or placing method) has changed and the revised calculation and check have not been completed.

posts.title: Sequence changes and temporary stability: CROSS learning for contractors

Sequence changes can remove the stability the permanent design assumed. CROSS reports show the pattern clearly.

CROSS-UK Report 1486 (published 20 November 2025) describes a partial collapse of underpinning overnight. Before excavation for a new section of underpinning, the principal contractor had removed portions of intermediate internal floors and walls to create workspace. Those elements had been providing restraint and load path. The building became unstable. The permanent works designer had already flagged the risk and asked for a temporary works design and close collaboration. No one was injured, but the Expert Panel noted the absence of an effective Temporary Works Coordinator role under BS 5975-1:2024 and the potential for HSE enforcement on the creation of risk, not only on harm.

CROSS-UK Report 1479 (published 13 January 2026) covers a late contractor change on a filler-beam bridge deck. Instead of lifting beams in connected pairs with precast concrete infill for temporary stability, beams were to be lifted individually. The Category II checker identified a risk of lateral-torsional buckling under wet concrete, with utilisation potentially exceeding 200%. Temporary LTB restraints became necessary. The issue was re-opened close to the pour, responsibility for the bracing design was unclear for a period, and the final design had to be produced under time pressure with reinforcement already fixed. Network Rail later issued engineering advice on temporary conditions.

These reports sit alongside recent HSE prosecutions in which temporary platforms and blockwork walls collapsed because there was no design, no calculation of loading, and no temporary works procedure or competent coordinator in place. CDM 2015 Regulation 19 requires that any new or existing structure is prevented from becoming unstable or remaining in a temporary state of weakness, and that temporary supports are designed, installed and maintained for the loads they will see. The duty is strict: if it is practicable, it must be done.

For principal contractors and Temporary Works Coordinators the practical controls remain straightforward:

- Treat any proposed change to sequence, removal of permanent elements, or alteration of temporary bracing as a change that must come through the Temporary Works Coordinator before work proceeds.
- Confirm that the temporary condition (including intermediate stages and overnight states) has been designed or checked, entered on the live Temporary Works Register with the correct category, and accepted under the project procedure.
- Do not remove floors, walls, props or bracing that form part of the current load path until the designer has confirmed the revised temporary works arrangement is in place and permitted.
- Require clear communication of design assumptions and restraints between permanent works and temporary works teams. Independent checking of change proposals remains essential.
- Where the permanent structure is being modified (underpinning, openings, partial demolition), the design brief must address both the structure itself and any adjacent buildings or highways that could be affected by movement.

Cause of the October 2026 partial collapse of the building and scaffolding under construction on Cherwell Street in Banbury remains under HSE investigation. No determination has been published. The incident continues to illustrate why sequence, bracing and load-path controls must be verified before work starts and again whenever the planned sequence changes.

Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1486 (published 20 November 2025) records a partial collapse of a section of underpinning overnight outside working hours. The collapse occurred during excavation for a new section of the underpinning process. Prior to the underpinning work the principal contractor had removed portions of intermediate internal floors and walls to create more workspace. These actions effectively destabilised the building. The permanent works designer had previously notified the client of the risks of removing critical permanent elements ahead of foundation work and had instructed that a temporary works design be commissioned with close collaboration with the principal contractor. The Expert Panel highlighted the importance of a clearly defined and agreed sequence, the potential loss of lateral restraint or load-bearing capacity from removed elements, the need for coordination between permanent and temporary works designers, and the likely value of a competent Temporary Works Coordinator fulfilling duties under BS 5975-1:2024. The Panel also noted that underpinning requires particular care with excavations left open overnight and that the event may justify HSE enforcement action on the creation of risk of harm. CDM 2015 Regulation 19 requires all practicable steps to ensure that any new or existing structure does not become unstable or remain in a temporary state of weakness, and that temporary supports are designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads.

body.h: Related CROSS learning on sequence change
body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1479 (published 13 January 2026) describes a late contractor change during design of an approximately 20 m span filler-beam bridge deck. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs (with concrete precast between pairs to provide temporary stability), the beams were to be lifted individually. The Category II checker identified that the main beams, if left unbraced and without rotational restraint at the ends of the flanges, could experience lateral-torsional buckling under the weight of wet concrete with a utilisation factor over 200%. Temporary LTB restraints were therefore required. The contractor’s temporary works design team initially took responsibility, but the necessity of the bracing was challenged again close to the pour. The final bracing design had to be produced under compressed programme with reinforcement already fixed. The Expert Panel noted vulnerability of single beams to LTB (including during lifting with possible load reversal), that plan bracing is generally required in addition to cross-bracing, the importance of clear communication of temporary conditions, and the value of independent checking. Network Rail subsequently produced a definition of temporary conditions and issued B&S Engineering advice note EAN03/2025 in September 2025.

Both reports illustrate the same temporary works failure mode: a change to sequence or removal of elements alters the temporary load path or restraint that the design (or previous stage) had assumed. In one case the outcome was a partial collapse; in the other it was identified as a near-miss by the independent checker. Recent HSE prosecutions involving collapsed temporary platforms and blockwork walls have similarly found absence of design, absence of loading calculations, and absence of a temporary works procedure or appointed coordinator. Under the project temporary works procedure and BS 5975-1:2024 any item that affects structural stability during construction must be entered on the Temporary Works Register, briefed against a design or confirmed standard solution, and subject to the required check category and permit regime. CDM 2015 places duties on principal contractors to plan, manage and monitor the work. Sequence changes and removal of permanent elements are classic points at which those duties are tested.

ul: Treat any proposed change to construction sequence, removal of permanent structural elements (floors, walls, beams), or alteration/removal of temporary bracing or props as a formal change that must be routed through the Temporary Works Coordinator before work proceeds.

Confirm that the temporary condition at every intermediate stage (including overnight and weather-exposed states) has been designed or checked by a competent person, entered on the live Temporary Works Register with the correct provisional design and check category, and accepted under the project procedure.

Do not allow removal of floors, walls, props or bracing that currently form part of the load path until the designer has confirmed that the revised temporary works arrangement is in place, checked and permitted.

Require explicit communication of design assumptions, required restraints and temporary conditions between the permanent works designer, temporary works designer and TWC. Independent checking of change proposals remains essential.

For underpinning, openings or partial demolition, ensure the design brief addresses both the structure being modified and any adjacent buildings, highways or services that could be affected by movement or loss of support.
Document the change control decision, the temporary works file entry and the permit status so the arrangement remains auditable.

If programme or commercial pressure is cited as a reason to proceed without the verified temporary works arrangement, escalate through the project temporary works procedure and the client; do not proceed.

body.p: On 12 November 2026 Lord Roe, Chair of the Building Safety Regulator, gave evidence to the Public Bill Committee examining the Building Safety (Remediation of Unsafe Cladding etc) Bill. He stated that the shortage of specialist contractors and façade engineers remains profound. When asked by Lewis Cocking MP whether the industry had enough qualified workers, he answered no. He said the skills problem had been built over decades through under-investment in construction skills and would take time to reverse. He added that the BSR would use its enforcement powers but would need to be pragmatic: if an applicant cannot obtain a specialist scaffolder because none is available in their area, or cannot find the right façade engineer, the regulator would adjust how it chases the application so as not to force engagement with poor or unskilled contractors. He noted that the BSR itself is competing for the same small pool of specialist engineers.

Cladding remediation on buildings over 11 m is a major programme. The access system is temporary works. Specialist scaffolding for these projects is not generic access; it involves complex configurations, public protection, load management for materials and plant, and interfaces with occupied buildings. Lord Roe’s evidence places the availability of competent scaffolders and façade engineers explicitly inside the enforcement discussion. A pragmatic approach by the regulator does not create an exemption from existing duties. Under CDM 2015 contractors must plan, manage and monitor the work. Under the project temporary works procedure and BS 5975-1:2024 the scaffolding design, its check category, the competence of the scaffolding contractor and the Temporary Works Supervisor must still be verified. Programme pressure or supply shortage cannot justify accepting an unsuitable contractor or an unverified temporary works arrangement.

ul: Treat the cladding remediation scaffold as a temporary works item requiring a design brief that covers height, configuration, loading (workers, materials, plant, wind), public interface, occupied building constraints and any special requirements for façade access.

Confirm the scaffolding contractor’s competence for the specific class of work (complex external remediation scaffolds) before appointment; do not rely on general CISRS cards alone if the project procedure requires additional evidence.
Enter the scaffold on the live Temporary Works Register with the correct design category and required check category (provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC).
Require a verified temporary works design (or confirmed standard solution where appropriate) and the independent check before any permit-to-erect or permit-to-load is issued.
Do not allow programme or remediation-target pressure to override the requirement for a competent contractor and an accepted temporary works arrangement.
Document the competence assessment and the decision path so that the temporary works file remains auditable if the regulator later reviews the project.

If a specialist scaffolder is genuinely unavailable, escalate the issue through the project temporary works procedure and the client; do not proceed with an alternative that lacks the required competence.

body.p: HSE press release dated 5 November 2026 records that AJ Riley Landscapes and Building Limited of Caton, Lancashire, was fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £4,955 in costs at Warrington Magistrates’ Court on 3 November 2026. Employee Josh Huddleston, 47, was replacing a damaged skylight on the roof of a barn on 24 February 2025 when he fell approximately 10 metres through the fragile roof. He suffered fractures to his ribs, vertebrae and pelvis. An HSE investigation found that the company had failed to adequately plan the work and ensure appropriate control measures were in place to prevent a fall through the fragile roof. The investigation also found that workers had not received sufficient training to ensure they were competent in the use of the control measures identified in the company’s risk assessment. The company pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. HSE inspector Matthew Shepherd noted that the risks of working at height on fragile roof surfaces are well known and that the incident could have been prevented through proper planning, risk assessment and effective control measures.

Fragile roofs and rooflights are a classic high-consequence work-at-height hazard. A fall of approximately 10 metres produced serious fractures; the outcome could easily have been fatal. The HSE findings point to two linked failures: inadequate planning of the work (so that suitable measures were not in place) and insufficient training so that workers were not competent to apply the controls listed in the company’s own risk assessment. Under the Work at Height Regulations 2005, work at height must be properly planned, appropriately supervised and carried out by competent people, and suitable and sufficient measures must be taken to prevent a fall. CDM 2015 places duties on contractors to plan, manage and monitor construction work so that it is carried out without risks to health and safety. For temporary works, any system used to provide access, distribute load, cover openings or protect against falls (crawl boards, temporary staging, netting, edge protection, covers) falls within the project temporary works procedure and BS 5975-1:2024 management framework. A paper risk assessment is not a substitute for a planned method, competent people and verified controls.

ul: Treat work on or near fragile roofs or rooflights as a temporary works activity requiring a design brief or confirmed standard solution, entry on the live Temporary Works Register, and acceptance under the project procedure before work starts.

Confirm the hierarchy of controls from HSG33 and the Work at Height Regulations 2005 has been applied: avoid the work if possible; otherwise use a safe system that prevents falls (e.g. roof ladders, crawl boards, temporary covers, netting, edge protection) rather than relying solely on personal fall-arrest.

Require the method statement or temporary works design to identify the specific fragile elements (skylights, cement sheets, rooflights), the access route, the load-spreading measures and how persons are prevented from stepping on unsupported fragile material.

Verify competence: the people carrying out the work must have received sufficient training in the control measures identified and must be supervised by a competent person. A risk assessment listing controls is not evidence of competence.
Ensure any temporary access equipment, covers or netting is suitable for the load, installed in accordance with the design or manufacturer instructions, and inspected before use.
Hold a permit-to-work or equivalent authorisation under the project temporary works procedure before anyone steps onto the roof. Do not allow work to start on the basis of an unreviewed method.
Record the planning, the competence check, the inspection of temporary measures and the acceptance so the file is auditable.

body.p: Marine Safety Forum Safety Alert 26-17, published 28 October 2026, records a high-potential incident on an offshore support vessel. A three-tier mobile scaffolding unit was being repositioned near the provisions-crane pedestal by the Bosun and an AB. Because the wheels were seized, the scaffold was dragged rather than rolled. When the unit reached a raised metal plate near a skylight it was lifted to continue the movement. It became unstable and collapsed, falling three deck levels to the main deck. No exclusion or drop zone had been established on the lower deck. No personnel were present below and no injuries were sustained. The alert does not name the vessel, operator or exact date of the incident.

Mobile scaffolds are temporary works equipment. Moving a multi-tier unit changes its stability and introduces a falling-object risk to anyone below. Seized wheels, ineffective brakes or unsecured locking pins increase the chance of loss of control. Lifting the unit over an obstruction further reduces stability. The absence of an exclusion zone meant the only reason there were no injuries was that no one happened to be below at the time. The same conditions can arise on a construction site when a mobile tower is repositioned for access, inspection or light work without a documented method, a confirmed fit-for-movement check, or a controlled drop zone. Under the Work at Height Regulations 2005 and the project temporary works procedure, the activity must be planned, supervised and controlled. BS 5975-1:2024 provides the management framework for temporary works, including items that may appear routine.

ul: Confirm the mobile scaffold is fit for movement before any handling: wheels free to roll, brakes effective, locking pins secured, overall stability adequate for the height and location.
Enter the mobile scaffold and any planned repositioning on the live Temporary Works Register where the project procedure requires it, and confirm the design category or manufacturer limits.
Require a task-specific method that identifies the path, any obstacles, the competence of the team and how an exclusion or drop zone will be established and maintained on levels below.
Do not drag a unit with seized wheels or lift it over obstructions without a reassessment and, if necessary, a revised method or additional controls.
Apply Stop Work if the task becomes difficult, the path changes, or the unit will not move as expected; reassess before continuing.
Ensure the Temporary Works Supervisor or a competent person verifies the exclusion zone and the condition of the scaffold before the move starts.
Record the check and the outcome so the temporary works file remains auditable.

posts.excerpt: CROSS-UK Report 1588 (3 November 2026) records a proposed change from sequential in-situ splicing of braced girder pairs to a single ground-spliced lift. A change to the lift sequence can rewrite the permanent works assumptions.

CROSS-UK Report 1588, published 3 November 2026, describes a 60 m steel girder bridge. The permanent works designer had designed on the basis that three girder sections would be braced in pairs, lifted, and spliced sequentially in situ. The contractor, with their temporary works designer, proposed instead to splice the three sections on the ground and undertake a single lift, with lifting points near the splices.

The permanent works calculation assumed the bolted splices would maintain friction-grip behaviour. The single-lift proposal relied on the connection plates shifting to engage the bolts in end bearing. Had it proceeded unchallenged, movement could have damaged the prepared faying surfaces, reducing long-term slip resistance and potentially affecting fatigue performance over the 120-year design life. The issue was identified because the contractor’s team followed the review processes in BS 5975 and PAS 8811 and engaged the permanent works designer before construction.

Under CDM 2015, specifying or modifying a construction method carries designer duties. Temporary conditions can be more onerous than the completed structure. Connections are frequent interfaces between permanent and temporary works designers. Confirm the permanent works assumptions (load path, connection behaviour, construction sequence) are explicit in the design brief. When the temporary works proposal changes that sequence, refer it back. Enter the lift, the temporary bracing or supports, and the splice condition on the live Temporary Works Register. Do not treat a practical-looking alternative lift as automatically compatible with the permanent works design.

body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1588, published 3 November 2026, concerns a proposed change to the construction sequence for erection of a 60 m steel girder bridge. The permanent works designer had designed the bridge on the basis that three girder sections would be braced in pairs, lifted, and spliced sequentially in situ after installation onto the supports. The contractor, working with their temporary works designer, proposed instead to splice the three sections together on the ground and undertake a single lift. The lifting points for the fully spliced girder were located near the spliced connections. This altered the loads expected to be transferred through the splice connections during installation.

A review by the permanent works designer identified that the permanent works calculation report assumed the bolted splice connections would maintain friction-grip behaviour. The single-lift proposal relied on the connection plates at the splice locations shifting during the lift to engage the bolts in end bearing. Had the proposal proceeded without challenge, movement at the splice interfaces could have damaged the prepared faying surfaces, reducing long-term slip resistance. While the bridge may have remained stable during erection, the permanent structural performance could have been compromised, with potential effects on fatigue performance over the structure’s 120-year design life. The critical permanent works assumptions were documented in the calculations but were not explicitly communicated through a risk register or clear notes on a drawing. The conflict was identified only because the contractor’s engineering team followed the review processes recommended in BS 5975 and PAS 8811 and engaged the permanent works designer before construction commenced. Under the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015, anyone specifying or modifying a construction method assumes designer responsibilities and must consider the consequences for both temporary and permanent works.

ul: Require the design brief for any major lift or erection sequence to state the permanent works designer’s assumed construction sequence, connection behaviour (e.g. friction-grip vs bearing) and any constraints on temporary loading or movement.
Enter the lift, temporary bracing or supports, and the temporary condition of the splices on the live Temporary Works Register before any alternative sequence is developed.
Where the temporary works proposal changes the sequence, load path or support arrangement assumed by the permanent works designer, refer the proposal back for assessment before acceptance.
Confirm that the temporary works design package addresses the behaviour of critical connections during the temporary condition and that any change in connection behaviour is explicitly accepted.
Treat a practical-looking alternative (ground assembly and single lift) as a design change that requires coordination, not merely a method change.
Record the engagement with the permanent works designer and the outcome in the temporary works file so the interface is auditable.
Do not proceed with the revised lift until the permanent works implications have been resolved and the register entry updated.

body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1613, published on 28 October 2026, records a chartered structural engineer’s report of multiple unauthorised changes during construction of an industrial building extension. Construction had commenced without planning approval, without a Building Regulations application, and without compliance with CDM. After a site inspection the Reporter identified numerous departures from the original design that had been implemented without consultation or design review. A steel grillage platform carrying approximately 5 tonnes of plant had been installed although it was not in the original design brief; the structure was erected before any design verification. The main steel frame had not accounted for the additional plant load. Subsequent checks showed that additional bracing was required to some posts. Other defects included alteration of gable frames to portal frames without review, an undesigned beam supporting a windpost, modified windpost head connections that transferred roof loads, bracing interrupted at a splice (leading to overstressed columns), undesigned column and windpost splices, omission of lower-level bracing for openings, uniform pad foundations with no evidence of design (inadequate for uplift in braced bays), and a retaining wall constructed without prior design.

Additional plant platforms, temporary stability bracing, load-path changes and undesigned connections are temporary works items or design-risk items under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015. Erecting them before verification places the load path outside the controlled design. The Expert Panel states that the number and extent of the changes are a significant cause for concern and that unauthorised alterations create a risk that safety-critical decisions are made without appropriate technical scrutiny. Where a contractor or others alter a design without obtaining approval from the original designer, they assume responsibility for those changes and the associated risks. Effective management of design changes relies on all dutyholders discharging their responsibilities under CDM 2015, including coordination of design and management of design risk. Seemingly minor changes can have significant implications for structural performance and temporary stability.

Confirm that the primary structure has been designed or checked for the additional loads and any change in load path or stability system.
Require formal design-change control: proposed changes must be reviewed and accepted by the responsible designer (or temporary works designer) before implementation.
Where design responsibilities are split, establish clear overall coordination so that the completed structure (permanent plus temporary) functions safely as a whole.
Use site inspections by a competent person (TWC or TWS) to identify departures from the approved design before they become embedded.
Record the residual risks and any remedial works required, and close the temporary works item only after verification and acceptance under the project procedure.

A Met Office gust is a meteorological observation. A temporary works design derives wind actions for a particular structure, location, height, terrain, geometry, exposure and period of use. Open scaffold, debris netting and full sheeting are not aerodynamically equivalent. Ties removed for façade work, added banners, altered hoarding or changed foundations can invalidate the checked arrangement.

BS 5975-1:2024 governs management procedures; BS 5975-2:2024 covers falsework design and implementation (including updated treatment of adjacent tall structures, funnelling and vortex shedding). NASC SG46:24 addresses adverse weather risk assessment, stopping and resuming work, and securing structures. HSE scaffolding guidance requires inspection after high winds by a competent person before normal use resumes.

body.p: Storm Austen produced an official UK peak gust of 76 mph on 23 October 2026. The Met Office recorded 76 mph at St Mary’s Airport on the Isles of Scilly, 75 mph at the Isle of Portland and Needles Old Battery, and 74 mph at Aberporth. Stronger unofficial readings were reported from some exposed coastal locations. London Construction Magazine used the event to explain why a recorded gust cannot be treated as a direct temporary works design check.

Site teams are frequently asked whether a scaffold, hoarding, temporary roof or falsework is “rated for 70 mph” or similar. Without the design basis that question cannot be answered. Wind design accounts for site location, terrain, altitude, topography, neighbouring buildings, height, exposed area, porosity and the intended duration. An open scaffold, a scaffold with debris netting and a fully sheeted scaffold are not equivalent. Added banners, temporarily removed ties, altered hoarding panels, materials stored on platforms never designed for them, or the loss of shielding from demolition can all change the condition assumed by the original design. BS 5975-2:2024 specifically addresses effects of adjacent tall structures, funnelling and vortex shedding for falsework. The design is only valid for the arrangement that was checked.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Identify temporary works particularly exposed to wind (tall scaffolds, sheeted or netted elevations, temporary roofs, hoardings, façade retention, large formwork and falsework).
Confirm that the temporary works register, approved design, inspection status and the arrangement actually standing on site still describe the same structure.

Verify that ties, bracing, anchors and foundations remain as designed. Any temporary removal of ties or restraint is a design change until the designer or competent person confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.

Establish whether sheeting, netting, banners or other surfaces have been added or altered since the design was checked. HSE scaffolding guidance is clear that sheeting or debris netting should not be attached without informing those responsible for the design.
Secure loose materials, boards and components that could become wind-borne. Follow any structure-specific or manufacturer operating restrictions.

Before severe wind, apply the project procedure for stopping or restricting work. NASC SG46:24 addresses weather-related risk assessment, stopping and resuming scaffold operations, inspection requirements and securing structures.

After high winds (or other circumstances liable to jeopardise safety), arrange inspection by a competent person appropriate to the type and complexity of the temporary works before normal use resumes. On scaffolding this includes ties, bracing, platforms, sheeting, base plates, sole boards and any evidence of movement or settlement. Heavy rain may also affect ground conditions under foundations even where no damage is obvious above ground.

Where a design assumption has changed, or where damage or partial dismantling leaves the installed arrangement different from the approved design, refer the issue back through the project temporary works procedure rather than resolving it informally on site.

body.p: BS 5975-1:2024 sets out management procedures for the control of temporary works. BS 5975-2:2024 covers falsework design and implementation; BSI notes that the 2024 revision calculates maximum wind forces on a likely erection duration of one year (reduced from two years) with a ten-year return period. First-generation Eurocodes, including BS EN 1991-1-4 for wind actions, remain the applicable UK standards for buildings and civil engineering works until 30 March 2028 unless a relevant authority or project specification requires otherwise. NASC TG20:21 provides recognised scaffold configurations; TG30:24 addresses operational guidance. NASC SG46:24 addresses adverse and inclement weather. HSE scaffolding guidance requires ties to remain within safe working limits and scaffolds to be checked when substantially altered or adversely affected, including by high winds. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copies.

It is subject to project-specific verification, the project temporary works procedure, and acceptance by the competent person (TWC) appointed under that procedure. posts.title: Scaffold dismantling: exclusion zones and controlled lowering after Belfast fatality
posts.excerpt: On 22 October 2026, 7 Towers Scaffolding Ltd was fined £20,000 after a collection driver was fatally struck by a metal scaffold board that fell about 8 m during dismantling on a Belfast site in December 2024. HSENI found the exclusion zone was not adequately controlled so that people not involved in the dismantling could approach. The case reinforces two basic temporary works controls: planned controlled lowering of components, and a physical exclusion zone that keeps everyone else out.

body.p: On 22 October 2026, 7 Towers Scaffolding Ltd (County Antrim) was fined £20,000 at Laganside Crown Court after previously pleading guilty to a single breach of Article 4(1) of the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978. On 18 December 2024, while a team was dismantling scaffold on a site on Lisburn Road, Belfast, a metal scaffolding board approximately 2.4 m long became dislodged from the upper part of the structure and fell about 8 m. It struck Samuel Magill, 60, a collection driver employed by the company who had arrived to collect dismantled components. He had parked on the pavement and walked toward the work area. He was struck at the outer edge of the site exclusion zone, next to the pavement. He died in hospital on 5 February 2025.

HSENI found that the company had not sufficiently managed and controlled the exclusion zone around the scaffolding during dismantling, so that people not directly involved in the work could approach. Inspector Kevin Campbell stated the incident was entirely preventable and that employers must ensure robust procedures so equipment and components are lowered to the ground in a controlled method, with clear work instructions communicated to all relevant personnel, and a clear identified exclusion zone with measures to prevent unauthorised persons entering. Scaffold dismantling is a temporary works activity. Falling objects and people entering the drop zone are foreseeable risks under the Work at Height Regulations and CDM 2015. Collection and delivery activity must be planned into the method, not treated as separate.

ul: Every scaffold (including system and tube-and-fitting) is entered on the Temporary Works Register with a named TWC, a design or TG20 compliance sheet, and an assembly, use and dismantling plan that specifically covers striking.
The dismantling plan requires controlled lowering of boards, tubes and fittings (gin wheel, hoist or equivalent). Throwing is not an acceptable method.

A physical exclusion zone is established below the work, clearly signed, and controlled by barriers or marshals so that drivers, other trades, visitors and the public cannot enter. The zone must account for the actual drop path, including items that can bounce or travel beyond the scaffold footprint.

Everyone who will be near the scaffold during dismantling — including collection drivers — is briefed on the zone and the method. A person whose role is to keep others out must not themselves be required to enter the zone.

Ties, bracing and platforms that maintain stability of the remaining scaffold are removed only in the planned sequence. Any departure is treated as a design change until the designer or competent person confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.
A competent person inspects the scaffold before dismantling starts and the permit-to-dismantle (or equivalent) is issued under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: BS 5975-1:2024 requires temporary works, including scaffolding, to be planned, designed (or covered by a standard solution), checked, registered and inspected. NASC TG20:21 and TG30:24 provide recognised configurations and operational guidance that include orderly dismantling from the top, retention of ties as long as possible, and the need for a plan. NASC SG4 addresses the scaffolders’ safe zone during erection and dismantling. HSE HSG150 (Health and safety in construction) addresses exclusion zones and preventing materials falling onto people. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copies.

posts.title: Banbury partial collapse: a prompt to re-check temporary stability controls
posts.excerpt: On 21 October a building under construction in Banbury partially collapsed with scaffolding. Two workers were hospitalised. HSE is investigating. Cause is not established. The incident is a prompt to re-confirm temporary works controls on sequence, bracing and load path — the same themes that appear in recent CROSS reports.
posts.linkedinReady:
On 21 October a building under construction on Lower Cherwell Street in Banbury partially collapsed with scaffolding. Nine workers were on site. Two were taken to hospital — one with head and leg injuries, one with severe injuries. HSE is investigating. No cause has been established and none is assumed here.

Incidents like this are a prompt, not a verdict. Structural stability during construction is a temporary-works issue until the permanent structure can stand on its own. Sequence changes, incomplete bracing, unassessed load paths into existing elements, and items treated as “just scaffolding” or “just temporary” sit in the same control space as the CROSS reports that keep appearing.

CROSS-UK Report 1479 (January 2026) is a clear recent example: a late contractor change from lifting beams in pairs to lifting them individually created a lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete that took utilisation over 200% without temporary restraints. The Category II check caught it. Many changes do not.

HSE’s structural stability guidance during alteration, demolition and dismantling is unchanged: temporary supports must be designed, installed and maintained for foreseeable loads, by people competent for the item. BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015 Regulation 19 still require the procedure — design brief, design and check, register, permit and competent inspection — not a verbal “it will be fine”.

Separately, Build UK’s Common Assessment Standard Version 6 (effective 1 November 2026) clarifies that scaffolding and temporary works do not fall within the Building Safety Regulations unless they form part of the completed structure. NASC welcomed the distinction. Competence requirements move, not disappear. The procedural controls under BS 5975 and CDM remain.

This week, for every live item that could affect stability:

- Confirm it is on the Temporary Works Register with a named TWC.
- Ask for the design (or documented standard solution), check category, permit and last competent inspection.
- Treat any sequence change or removal of bracing/props as a design change until the designer confirms otherwise.
- Check the full load path, including existing structure that will take redistributed load.

body.p: On Wednesday 21 October 2026 a partial collapse involving a building under construction and associated scaffolding occurred on Lower Cherwell Street in Banbury, Oxfordshire. The site is the redevelopment of a former car sales premises into 19 apartments. Thames Valley Police stated that nine workers were on site; two sustained injuries and were taken to hospital (one with head and leg injuries, one described as severe). There were no reports of anyone trapped. HSE confirmed it is aware of the incident and an investigation is underway. No cause has been established in the published reports.

body.h: Why this is a temporary works prompt
body.p: Until the permanent structure is self-stable, construction sequence, temporary bracing, propping, scaffolding interfaces and any alteration to the load path are temporary works. HSE guidance on structural stability during alteration, demolition and dismantling states that temporary supports must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads, and that structures should never be overloaded. Items that affect stability belong on the Temporary Works Register under the project procedure (BS 5975-1:2024).

CROSS-UK Report 1479 (published 13 January 2026) describes a late contractor change on a filler-beam bridge deck. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs, beams were to be lifted individually. This introduced a significant temporary stability risk of lateral-torsional buckling under the weight of wet concrete. Assessment showed utilisation exceeding 200% without rotational restraint and temporary LTB restraints. The Category II checker identified the issue; temporary restraints were required. The report notes that late changes to construction sequence can introduce significant temporary stability risks and that the Temporary Works Coordinator role must ensure clarity of design responsibility at each stage.

Build UK has announced that Version 6 of the Common Assessment Standard takes effect on 1 November 2026. Revisions to the Building Safety section reflect that scaffolding and temporary works no longer fall within the scope of the Building Safety Regulations unless they form part of the completed structure. NASC welcomed the clarification after seeking confirmation from MHCLG. Companies will opt out of the Building Safety section where it does not apply, with a confirming statement. Competence-based questions previously in Section 7 move into the quality section so they remain required. This does not remove the need for competence or for the procedural controls in BS 5975 and CDM 2015.

body.h: What a competent TWC / site team should confirm this week
ul: Every item that can affect structural stability during construction (scaffolding that is load-bearing or tied in a way that affects the permanent structure, temporary bracing, propping, sequence-critical elements) is on the Temporary Works Register with a named Temporary Works Coordinator.
There is a design or documented standard solution, an appropriate design check, a permit-to-load/use and a recent inspection by a person competent for that item.

Any proposed change to sequence, removal of bracing or props, or alteration of loading is treated as a design change and is not implemented until the temporary works designer confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.
The full load path has been considered, including existing structure that will carry redistributed load (see also CROSS-UK Report 1539).

body.p: On 14 October 2026 Construction Magazine / London Construction Magazine published “Before Scaffolding Is Erected: The Temporary Works Checks That Matter”. The article states that before a scaffold is erected the project team needs to know more than its height, length and intended access route. A scaffold can be correctly designed in isolation and still be unsuitable for the site if the ground, supporting structure, façade, services, attachments or future alterations do not match the assumptions used in that design. Problems commonly arise when elements are considered separately: leg loads bearing over a basement or void, increased reactions from a loading bay, mismatched tie patterns after façade removal, or wind actions from sheeting or temporary roofs that were not in the original brief. The current management procedures for temporary works are set out in BS 5975-1:2024. For project teams operating a BS 5975 procedure, the design brief is the point where requirements and interfaces should be captured before design progresses. Pre-erection checks cover design status (compliance sheet or project-specific design and check), intended loading, maximum leg reactions, foundation condition (including subsurface features), ties and anchors matched to the actual façade, attachments that affect loading or wind, site interfaces, and a change-control process.

Scaffolding is temporary works. HSE scaffolding guidance requires a scaffold either to follow a recognised standard configuration or, where it falls outside such a configuration, to be designed by calculation by a competent person. The foundation must be capable of carrying the scaffold and the loads placed on it; basements, drains and patches of soft ground that may collapse when loaded are specifically highlighted. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. BS 5975-1:2024 provides the industry framework for temporary works management procedures (it is not a statute). Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. The design brief is the control point that brings together use, loads, reactions, ground or structural support, ties, attachments and foreseeable change so that the load path from the scaffold through bases and ties into the supporting ground or structure is coherent. Standard does not automatically mean low risk when site conditions differ from the assumptions behind a standard configuration. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Capture in the design brief the intended use, loading class, boarded lifts, material storage, loading bays, ties, sheeting/netting, hoists, debris chutes, temporary roofs, ground conditions, subsurface features, façade type and any planned alterations before design or erection proceeds.
Confirm design status: either a recognised standard configuration whose assumptions are valid for the site, or a project-specific design and independent check by a competent person.

Obtain maximum leg reactions (including concentrated loads) and assess the supporting ground or structure. Treat basements, drains, manholes, voids, soft patches or recently backfilled ground as requiring specific assessment rather than assuming surface adequacy.
Verify that the tie strategy matches the actual façade, including openings, curtain walling, weak masonry or planned removals. Confirm anchor type, substrate suitability and any testing requirements.
Identify attachments (sheeting, netting, hoists, loading bays, fans, temporary roofs) as design inputs so that their effect on reactions, wind loading and restraint is allowed for before erection.

Establish change control so that any alteration to geometry, loading, restraint, exposure, foundations or supporting structure is referred to the Temporary Works Coordinator and re-checked where necessary before it is adopted.
Where the scaffold interfaces with public highways, excavations, deliveries or other temporary works, confirm licences, clearances and sequencing are compatible with the checked arrangement.

At permit-to-load or equivalent, confirm that the erected arrangement matches the design brief and checked design, including foundations, ties and attachments. Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

It is not a design, a check or a statement that any particular scaffold arrangement is adequate or inadequate. No reactions, ground capacities or tie loads have been calculated here. Subject to project-specific verification and acceptance under the project temporary works procedure. AI-assisted drafting requires competent review before use on site.
